title: Elbow Pain - Olecranon Bursitis (Excluding Septic Bursitis)
patient_instructions: You are Robert Fields, a 52-year-old plumber. Over the last 3 days you have developed a painful, red, swollen lump at the tip of your right elbow. It feels warm and tender and is squishy/fluid-like. It hurts to lean on it or bend the elbow fully. If asked: you feel generally OK but think you may have felt slightly feverish yesterday. There was no major injury, though you often lean on your elbows at work. You have a history of gout (a couple of big-toe attacks) and you had red wine and a big steak dinner two nights ago. If asked about triggers: yes, alcohol and red meat. You have NO chest pain, no arm pain radiating from the chest, no breathlessness. No numbness or tingling in the hand. No morning stiffness lasting hours, no other joints affected, no weight loss. You take no regular medications. Your ideas: you think your gout has 'gone to the elbow'. Your concerns: it is getting more red and sore and you wonder if it is infected. Your expectation: you want it fixed. You are cooperative. If asked whether it is hot/red and whether you feel unwell, emphasise the redness, warmth and the feverish feeling yesterday.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Robert Fields, 52, presents with 3 days of a painful, red, warm, fluctuant swelling over the tip of the right elbow. He has a history of gout. In 8 minutes: take a focused history, explain your differential diagnosis to the patient, and outline your initial investigation and management plan including safety-netting. The examiner will show/describe examination findings at 6 minutes.
examiner_instructions: This tests recognition that a hot, tender, fluctuant olecranon bursa may be SEPTIC bursitis, which cannot be distinguished clinically from gouty/crystal bursitis. At 6 minutes describe: a fluctuant, erythematous, warm, tender olecranon swelling; low-grade fever. Reward a candidate who plans bursal aspiration for MC&S, Gram stain and crystal examination BEFORE deciding treatment, and who states empirical antibiotics per eTG (e.g. di/flucloxacillin) only after aspiration if infection is suspected. Reward serum urate (noting it is often normal during an acute flare), FBC/CRP, and plain elbow X-ray if trauma. Reward non-septic management (rest, avoid pressure/leaning, compression, NSAID or paracetamol, aspiration if tense; treat underlying gout) and red-flag safety-netting including referred cardiac ischaemia (advise 000 if chest pain/breathlessness). Prompt: 'What is the single not-to-be-missed diagnosis here and how would you exclude it?'

criteria: Characterises the swelling (onset, warmth, redness, fluctuance, pain, trauma/pressure) and systemic symptoms (fever/malaise)
Takes a gout history (previous attacks, alcohol/red meat triggers) and screens inflammatory arthritis features
Screens red flags: fever/systemic sepsis, and referred causes of arm pain (cardiac ischaemia, Pancoast tumour)
Identifies olecranon bursitis as the diagnosis and lists septic vs crystal (gouty) bursitis as the leading acute causes
States septic and gouty bursitis cannot be distinguished clinically
Includes wider differential (septic arthritis of the elbow, epicondylitis) appropriately
Plans bursal aspiration for MC&S, Gram stain and crystal examination before deciding treatment; serum urate, FBC/CRP; X-ray if trauma
Empirical antibiotics per eTG (e.g. di/flucloxacillin) only after aspiration if infection suspected; non-septic care = rest, avoid pressure, compression, NSAID/paracetamol, treat gout
Safety-nets worsening sepsis and referred cardiac ischaemia (call 000 for chest pain/breathlessness)
Explains the diagnosis and need to sample the fluid in lay terms
Checks understanding and gives clear follow-up/safety-net advice

red_flags: Septic olecranon bursitis - hot, red, tender, fluctuant bursa with fever: aspirate before treating and cover with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics if infection suspected
Septic arthritis of the elbow (joint effusion, severe pain on any movement, systemic upset)
Referred cardiac ischaemia presenting as left arm pain - advise urgent 000 if chest pain/breathlessness develops
Pancoast (apical lung) tumour causing shoulder/medial arm and C8-T1 pain with Horner syndrome and intrinsic hand wasting
australian_guidelines: eTG: a hot, tender, fluctuant olecranon bursa should be aspirated for MC&S, Gram stain and crystal examination before deciding management; empirical antibiotics (e.g. di/flucloxacillin) only when infection is suspected
eTG gout: serum urate is often normal during an acute flare, so a normal urate does not exclude gout; manage acute gout and address alcohol/red-meat and other triggers
Non-septic olecranon bursitis management: rest, avoid pressure/leaning on the elbow, compression, NSAID or paracetamol, and aspiration if the bursa is tense
RACGP: screen not-to-be-missed causes of limb pain including referred cardiac ischaemia and apical lung (Pancoast) tumour
learning_objectives: Recognise septic olecranon bursitis as the key not-to-be-missed diagnosis in a hot fluctuant bursa
Aspirate and investigate before treating, and prescribe antibiotics appropriately per eTG
Distinguish and manage crystal (gouty) versus septic bursitis and treat the underlying gout
Safety-net referred cardiac and apical lung causes of arm pain
key_points: Septic and gouty olecranon bursitis cannot be distinguished clinically - aspirate for MC&S, Gram stain and crystals before treating
Serum urate is often normal during an acute gout flare
Antibiotics (e.g. di/flucloxacillin) only if infection is suspected after aspiration
Non-septic care: rest, avoid leaning on the elbow, compression, NSAID/paracetamol, treat gout
Always consider referred cardiac ischaemia and Pancoast tumour in upper-limb pain

citations.claim: Gout is a key differential for acute monoarticular limb pain and is prone to recurrence, supporting screening for red-meat/alcohol triggers.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.717

citations.claim: Inflammatory arthritis presents with prolonged morning stiffness, soft joint swelling and systemic features, underpinning inflammatory-vs-mechanical pattern questions.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.705

citations.claim: Red-flag pointers for upper-limb pain include fever (septic arthritis/osteomyelitis), redness/swelling and trauma, and serious not-to-be-missed causes include Pancoast tumour and cardiac ischaemia.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1481
